recent_publications.title: Perceive with confidence: Statistical safety assurances for navigation with learning-based perception
recent_publications.venue: International Journal of Robotics Research 45(6), 938–967 (first online 2025; issue May 2026)
recent_publications.assessment: Conformal calibration estimates perception uncertainty while accounting for planner-induced state shifts. The abstract reports simulation and quadruped navigation in unseen static indoor environments, with improved empirical safety. The statistical guarantee depends on the method's assumptions; this evidence does not establish safety in arbitrary dynamic or outdoor settings. Review depth: institutional abstract and publisher metadata; proofs, trial counts and code were not independently audited.
reading_questions: What calibration and distribution assumptions underpin the guarantee?
How are planner-induced state shifts handled?
How many physical trials were run, and which failure cases remain?

recent_publications.title: Function Encoders: A Principled Approach to Transfer Learning in Hilbert Spaces
recent_publications.venue: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 267:26464–26489
recent_publications.assessment: A peer-reviewed ICML paper on transfer learning: a learned function basis and least-squares fitting support adaptation, with a universal approximation theorem and comparisons against transformers and meta-learning on four benchmarks. This is useful mathematical and empirical evidence for adaptable learned dynamics; the abstract does not establish physical robot validation or safety guarantees. Review depth: publisher abstract and bibliographic metadata; proof assumptions and benchmark fairness were not independently audited.
reading_questions: Which assumptions make transfer to an unseen function possible?
How representative are the training functions and test shifts?
Does the approach preserve stability or safety when used inside a controller?

guide.thesis: Your strongest bridge is learning-enabled control of physical robots: keep dynamics, estimation and optimization as your technical foundation, then choose between aerospace missions, field autonomy and general-purpose manipulation. Youngwoon Lee’s work expands the last branch substantially.
guide.interpretation: These are reading priorities based on stated interests and public research evidence, not a ranking of intelligence, mentoring quality, admission probability or every professor’s ability. The full inventory in this atlas remains available beside this curated starting map.

tracks.title: Spacecraft, launch and mission GNC
tracks.question: How do we navigate and control a real vehicle under mission, uncertainty and compute constraints?
tracks.methods: Orbital/rigid-body dynamics, state estimation, convex/nonlinear optimization, MPC, robust/adaptive control, flight software.
tracks.departments: Aerospace, mechanical, electrical/control, astronomy/satellite systems, applied mathematics.
tracks.fit: Best continuity with classical GNC and a dynamics/control portfolio. Flight heritage and validated estimation matter more here than raw AI citation counts.
tracks.project: Build a six-degree-of-freedom rendezvous or landing simulation; compare a baseline controller with constrained MPC; report dispersions, timing, infeasibility and recovery.

tracks.title: Aerial, mobile and field autonomy
tracks.question: How can a robot perceive, plan and act reliably outside a clean laboratory?
tracks.methods: SLAM, visual/inertial navigation, perception-aware planning, MPC, learning-based adaptation, multi-robot coordination.
tracks.departments: Aerospace, robotics, CS, ECE, ME, civil/infrastructure and field-engineering groups.
tracks.fit: A close bridge between GNC and autonomy. Separate papers with physical flight/field deployments from simulation-only navigation.
tracks.project: Implement perception-aware navigation with a documented compute budget. Evaluate estimator drift, changing lighting/terrain, interruptions and recovery, not only average success.

tracks.title: Safe learning and control theory
tracks.question: When can learning improve performance while preserving a defensible safety or stability statement?
tracks.methods: Reachability, control barrier functions, Lyapunov methods, formal methods, uncertainty quantification, safe RL, policy optimization.
tracks.departments: EE/control, aerospace, robotics, applied mathematics, systems and industrial engineering.
tracks.fit: Strong option if you enjoy proofs and optimization as much as robotics. A safety claim is conditional on model, sensing, disturbance and computation assumptions.
tracks.project: Combine a learned policy with a safety filter. State the assumptions and test violations, latency, feasibility, conservatism and baseline controller performance.

tracks.title: Robot learning, manipulation and embodied AI
tracks.question: How can a robot acquire reusable skills from demonstrations, video, language, simulation and interaction?
tracks.methods: Imitation learning, RL, diffusion policies, vision-language-action models, world models, tactile perception, scalable data collection.
tracks.departments: CS/AI, robotics, ECE, ME and interdisciplinary AI institutes.
tracks.fit: Closest to the supplied Youngwoon Lee example. Look for a coherent technical contribution and reproducible physical evaluation; larger models and datasets are not enough by themselves.
tracks.project: Reproduce a manipulation policy, then test one precise generalization question with equal data and compute budgets. Report failed trials and distribution shifts; release a reproducible training/evaluation configuration.

tracks.title: Legged robots, humanoids and physical interaction
tracks.question: How should whole-body motion, contact and manipulation be learned and controlled together?
tracks.methods: Rigid-body/contact dynamics, trajectory optimization, whole-body control, sim-to-real RL, tactile interaction, co-design.
tracks.departments: Mechanical, robotics, CS, electrical and biomechanics.
tracks.fit: Combines the user’s dynamics/control interest with modern robot learning. Hardware availability, maintenance burden and access to experiments are practical advisor-selection criteria.
tracks.project: Compare model-based and learned controllers under contact uncertainty. Track recovery, hardware interventions, energy/torque limits and transfer across surfaces or payloads.

venues.names: IEEE TAC; Automatica; SIAM Journal on Control and Optimization
venues.assessment: Strong specialist homes for mathematical control research. Look for a substantive theorem, meaningful assumptions and a clear advance over prior results. Purely theoretical work can be excellent without hardware experiments.

venues.names: IEEE TCST; AIAA Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics; Journal of the Astronautical Sciences
venues.assessment: Directly relevant to implementation and aerospace dynamics/GNC. Examine realistic vehicle models, uncertainty, implementation cost, hardware/flight evidence and operational constraints.

venues.names: IEEE Transactions on Robotics; IJRR; Science Robotics; IEEE RA-L; Journal of Field Robotics
venues.assessment: Established robotics outlets with different article lengths and aims. RA-L is a peer-reviewed journal, and a RA-L paper presented at ICRA/IROS should not be counted as two independent papers.

Main-conference papers are central research outputs in robotics. Venue is a useful screening signal, but compare evidence, novelty and relevance. An award is additional evidence, not a guarantee of every subsequent result.

venues.names: NeurIPS; ICML; ICLR; CVPR; ICCV; ECCV
venues.assessment: Highly relevant to learning, representation and embodied AI. Verify the track and whether the paper actually evaluates physical robot behavior. Datasets/benchmarks, surveys and methods papers answer different questions.

venues.names: arXiv; workshop papers; posters; invited talks
venues.assessment: Useful for the newest direction, but acceptance and review depth must be established separately. A workshop award is not a main-conference best-paper award. A preprint is not a poor paper; its external review status is simply different.

quality_rubric.check: Can you state the new idea, theorem, algorithm or system capability precisely? Compare with the strongest relevant prior work, not only weak baselines.

For theory: inspect assumptions and proof coverage. For systems: inspect physical trials, interventions, failure distributions and robustness. For learning: inspect data/compute parity, unseen-task tests, leakage and uncertainty.
Look for code, data, configurations, hardware details, evaluation scripts and clear failure reporting. Public code is a positive signal, not proof that results reproduce.
Read at least two recent student-led papers and one foundational lab paper. Determine whether your desired project sits in the lab’s current research program rather than an old collaboration.

Check who leads papers, time to first meaningful contribution, alumni trajectories, coadvising and access to facilities. Publications and citations cannot establish mentoring style; ask current students directly.

Confirm that the PI can supervise through your intended degree, is accepting students, has suitable funding and can provide the equipment/data access your project requires. Unknown is not a negative judgment.

application_steps: Choose one primary track and one adjacent track; retain a broad inventory but develop a technically coherent application story.
Use the atlas to select roughly 12–20 labs for deep reading. Read two recent papers and one foundational paper per lab before narrowing the final application set.
For each target, write a short research-fit note: the problem you want to solve, one result you understand, a concrete limitation and a feasible next experiment or theorem.
Build one rigorous project with transparent baselines, failures and reproducible code. For GNC/autonomy, demonstrate dynamics and estimation competence alongside learning.
Use the official admissions route for the actual degree and department. Recruiting notices are snapshots; do not infer deadlines or funded positions from an old lab page.

Follow the PI’s contact instructions. Levine and Gupta explicitly ask prospective PhD applicants not to email directly; other groups invite contact. A documented coauthor/advisor link is an intellectual connection, not a promised introduction.

Before committing, discuss supervision frequency, student ownership, funding duration, publication expectations, hardware access and alumni outcomes with the PI and current students. Do not infer these from prestige.
limits: The university universe is bounded and enumerated. The faculty inventory is a large evidence-backed search, not a certified proof that no relevant lab exists beyond it. Each university records the directories checked and the unresolved departments or profiles.

Publication attached means a specific recent paper was identified. It does not mean every paper was read in full, reproduced, or critically reviewed. Paper assessments state the reading depth where available.

Citation counts use dated, named providers. OpenAlex and institutional counts are not interchangeable with Google Scholar; missing is not zero. OpenAlex identities were sampled against known works and affiliations, not exhaustively audited across every work.

Recent means generally 2023–2026 in this snapshot, with older foundational work only when explicitly labeled. Accepted/to-appear work is distinct from published work; future events are not described as already held.
QS overall is the user-selected eligibility rule. It is not a lab-quality score and excludes some excellent specialist institutions. Korea is restricted to the four explicitly selected universities.
Student recruiting, mentoring, funding and application deadlines remain unknown unless a current source explicitly states them. No emails or applications have been sent.

chapters.title: Dynamics and feedback control
chapters.subtitle: How actions change a physical system—and how feedback corrects them
chapters.question: What must be true before a robot can reliably track a command?
chapters.summary: Control starts with a causal model of motion and a precise objective. A controller repeatedly converts available information into actions, so its behavior depends on the plant, sensors, actuator limits and timing together. This chapter supplies the language needed to judge both hand-designed controllers and learned policies.

sections.heading: State, dynamics and the boundary of the model
sections.text: A state summarizes the past information needed to predict the future under specified inputs. For a pendulum, angle alone is insufficient: angular velocity matters too. Write continuous dynamics as ẋ = f(x,u,w), with state x, commanded input u and disturbance w; measurements satisfy y = h(x) plus sensor error. Choosing a state is a modeling decision. Motor lag, joint flexibility or sensor bias may need extra states when they affect the time scale of the task.

sections.heading: Feedback is an information loop
sections.text: An open-loop command is fixed without correcting measured deviations. Feedback changes the command when the observed behavior differs from the objective. Proportional action responds to present error, integral action accumulates persistent error, and derivative action anticipates its change. Integral action can remove a constant offset but wind up under saturation; differentiating noisy measurements can amplify noise. A good PID baseline therefore includes filtering, actuator limits and anti-windup, rather than only three tuned gains.

sections.heading: Local models reveal what can be controlled
sections.text: Linearization approximates deviations around an equilibrium or reference trajectory: δẋ = Aδx + Bδu. Its usefulness depends on how far the real motion leaves that neighborhood. Controllability asks whether inputs can move the state in every direction; stabilizability asks the weaker, often sufficient question of whether unstable modes can be controlled. Underactuation is different: fewer independent inputs than mechanical degrees of freedom does not automatically imply uncontrollability. A cart can balance a pole through dynamic coupling.

sections.heading: Stability is a claim with a domain
sections.text: Lyapunov stability means sufficiently small initial errors remain small; asymptotic stability additionally means they converge to zero. Exponential stability specifies a decay rate. A Lyapunov function is an energy-like scalar whose change constrains trajectories, so one need not solve every trajectory explicitly. For nonlinear systems, the certified region of attraction matters as much as the theorem. A controller that balances a nearly upright pendulum may have no ability to recover it from hanging downward.

sections.heading: Two complementary views of the same loop
sections.text: State-space methods expose internal dynamics, multivariable coupling and unmeasured states. Frequency-response methods expose how disturbances and sensor noise are amplified at different frequencies. Nyquist analysis and gain/phase margins explain why a loop with good low-frequency tracking can oscillate when delay grows. Neither viewpoint replaces the other. An observer can reconstruct missing state information under observability assumptions, but its dynamics and noise sensitivity must be included when assessing the complete closed loop.

sections.heading: From equations to an autonomous machine
sections.text: A simulation controller often receives perfect state at exactly spaced times. A deployed controller receives delayed, noisy estimates and may miss deadlines. Record the sample period, computation latency, command hold, saturation and coordinate conventions explicitly. Learning changes how a policy is obtained; it does not remove these constraints. The most useful early research habit is to explain a failure through the closed-loop mechanism: poor model, weak observability, insufficient control authority, unsuitable objective or timing error.

open_questions: How much physical state must a learned policy represent to remain reliable under delay and partial observation?
Can controller simplicity be traded systematically against certified operating range?
pitfalls: Treating local stability as global recovery.
Comparing algorithms while giving one perfect state or a faster control rate.
Equating low tracking error with low effort, robustness or safety.

project.title: A controller that survives imperfect sensing
project.description: Build a torque-limited pendulum simulation. Compare PD, PID and local linear feedback around the upright equilibrium. Add an observer, measurement noise and command delay one at a time, then explain the changes using dynamics and feedback rather than only plotting rewards.
evaluation: Map successful initial conditions.
Report tracking error, peak torque and saturation time.
Sweep delay and sensor-noise levels with identical trials.

sources.label: Åström and Hägglund: automatic PID tuning

chapters.title: Bayesian estimation and navigation
chapters.subtitle: Turning imperfect measurements into a useful belief about motion
chapters.question: Where is the robot, how uncertain is that answer, and does the uncertainty matter for the next action?
chapters.summary: Navigation is an inference problem before it is a control problem. Sensors measure projections of the world, not a complete state. Estimation combines those measurements with motion models and prior information, while uncertainty describes what remains unresolved. A precise estimate with unjustified confidence can be more dangerous than an openly uncertain one.

sections.heading: Prediction and correction
sections.text: A Bayesian filter maintains a distribution over the current state conditioned on measurements and past actions. Prediction propagates that distribution through a dynamics model; correction multiplies it by the likelihood of a new observation and normalizes. The model may include position, velocity, attitude, sensor biases and unknown environmental quantities. Conditional-independence assumptions make this recursion tractable, but they must match the sensor pipeline: repeatedly using correlated observations as independent evidence creates false confidence.

sections.heading: What the Kalman filter actually guarantees
sections.text: For a linear system with Gaussian initial state and appropriate Gaussian process and measurement noise, the Kalman filter represents the exact posterior using a mean and covariance. Without Gaussianity, its familiar optimality is among linear estimators under the relevant second-moment assumptions. The covariance is not a universal measure of truth; it is conditional on the chosen model and noise statistics. Unmodeled bias, incorrect timestamps or an erroneous measurement association can invalidate its apparent precision.

sections.heading: Nonlinearity requires an approximation choice
sections.text: An extended Kalman filter linearizes dynamics and measurements around an estimate. An unscented filter propagates selected points to approximate moments. Particle methods represent distributions with weighted samples and can retain multiple hypotheses, but their computational burden grows rapidly when useful samples become rare. These are different approximations, not a ranking in which a newer method always wins. Initialization, observability, outlier handling and sensor calibration can dominate the difference between algorithms.

sections.heading: Geometry and observability
sections.text: Orientation lives on a curved space: adding three numbers to a rotation is generally not a globally valid update. Error-state and invariant filters separate a geometric state from a local error description. Barrau and Bonnabel show why exploiting group structure can produce useful stability properties for a particular class of systems; the result is not a guarantee for every nonlinear filter. Also distinguish uncertainty from gauge freedom: a mapping system may lack absolute position or yaw information even while relative motion is well estimated.

sections.heading: Filtering versus smoothing
sections.text: Filtering estimates the present using data available now; smoothing revises past states when later measurements arrive. Factor graphs express a trajectory estimate through local constraints from sensors and motion. iSAM2 updates a sparse factorization incrementally, while IMU preintegration compresses many inertial readings into a keyframe-to-keyframe constraint with bias corrections. These mechanisms make large estimation problems practical, but neither makes an incorrect loop closure or a wrong measurement model harmless.

sections.heading: The estimate must serve the task
sections.text: A navigation system should be evaluated for both accuracy and consistency. Check whether reported uncertainty matches observed errors, whether failures are detected, and how estimates behave during sensor dropout. Active perception then closes another loop: choose actions that improve information, such as moving to create parallax. Planning with a belief can preserve visibility or reduce uncertainty before a difficult maneuver. This connects estimation to decision-making; it also explains why optimizing pose error alone can miss operational failure.

open_questions: How can learned measurement models produce uncertainty that remains calibrated after deployment shift?
How should planning balance immediate progress against improving observability?
pitfalls: Reporting only mean trajectory error while ignoring rare divergence.
Treating filter covariance as a ground-truth error bound.
Using future measurements in an evaluation advertised as online navigation.

project.title: Filtering and smoothing under biased sensors
project.description: Simulate a ground robot with wheel odometry, an IMU and intermittent landmark observations. Implement an EKF and a small fixed-window smoother using the same measurements. Introduce bias, dropout and wrong associations separately, and identify which model changes or rejection mechanisms resolve each failure.
evaluation: Compare trajectory error and uncertainty coverage.
Measure latency and memory as the trajectory grows.
Report recovery behavior after dropout and bad measurements.

chapters.title: Robust, adaptive and nonlinear control
chapters.subtitle: Designing for uncertainty without hiding the assumptions
chapters.question: What changes when the model is wrong, the operating point moves, or the environment changes?
chapters.summary: These methods address different problems. Robust control protects against a specified uncertainty family; adaptive control updates a model or controller from data; nonlinear control reasons directly about dynamics that a single linear approximation cannot capture. They can be combined, but a claim from one framework cannot be transferred to another without checking its assumptions.

sections.heading: Begin by naming the uncertainty
sections.text: An unknown but constant payload differs from a rapidly changing disturbance, a delayed measurement, and an unmodeled flexible mode. Write down whether uncertainty is bounded, probabilistic, structured, matched to the actuator channel, or unrestricted. A robust statement is meaningful only relative to that description. Making the uncertainty set larger often protects more scenarios while reducing performance or eliminating feasibility. Underestimating it can produce a beautiful certificate for a system that does not describe the experiment.

sections.heading: Robust performance versus average performance
sections.text: H-infinity control limits the worst-case amplification from specified disturbance inputs to regulated outputs for the modeled system. H2 and LQG formulations instead connect to energy or variance objectives under their respective assumptions. The distinction matters: a controller with excellent average behavior may respond poorly to a carefully aligned disturbance. Weighting functions encode which frequencies and outputs matter, so they are part of the design claim. A robust synthesis result is not protection against arbitrary damage, arbitrary delays or unconstrained errors.

sections.heading: Adaptation needs information
sections.text: Adaptive control adjusts parameters online to improve tracking despite uncertain dynamics. Slotine and Li's manipulator controller uses mechanical structure to combine feedback with an adaptive dynamics term. Small tracking error does not necessarily mean the estimated physical parameters are correct: several parameter combinations may explain the motion, and informative excitation may be absent. Persistent excitation is therefore an identification condition, not simply another name for stability. Fast adaptation also interacts with noise, saturation and unmodeled dynamics.

sections.heading: Nonlinear control offers several kinds of certificate
sections.text: Feedback linearization cancels modeled nonlinearities, so its usefulness depends on model accuracy, relative degree and internal dynamics. Lyapunov design seeks a scalar function that decreases along controlled trajectories. Sontag's construction shows how a suitable control-Lyapunov function can generate stabilizing feedback, but finding the function and accommodating actuator limits remain substantive tasks. Energy shaping exploits mechanical structure. These methods are ways to organize a proof and a design, rather than interchangeable algorithm names.

sections.heading: Contraction asks about trajectories, not only equilibria
sections.text: Contraction analysis studies whether neighboring trajectories move toward one another under a suitable metric. This can simplify tracking and observer reasoning because convergence can be studied separately from a particular equilibrium. The hard part moves to finding and validating the metric over the required domain. Local contraction in a training region does not imply global convergence, and a continuous-time differential condition needs care when the implementation samples, switches modes or experiences impacts.

sections.heading: Learning can supply models or certificates
sections.text: A neural network can estimate a residual dynamics term, propose a Lyapunov function, or directly generate a control policy. These roles require different evidence. A small prediction error on a held-out data set is not itself a closed-loop guarantee; conversely, a certificate verified over a restricted region need not make the policy competent outside it. Separate the learned candidate from the verification mechanism. Ask whether inequalities were tested on samples, bounded over a continuum, or formally checked with explicit numerical tolerances.

open_questions: How can online adaptation expand useful operating range while preserving constraints throughout learning?
Which uncertainty descriptions remain credible when perception and dynamics are both learned?
pitfalls: Claiming parameter convergence from tracking convergence alone.
Treating successful random perturbations as a worst-case proof.
Canceling dynamics without checking actuator limits or unstable internal dynamics.

project.title: Payload changes without hidden retuning
project.description: Compare fixed-gain, robustly tuned and adaptive controllers on a two-link arm with uncertain payload. Freeze the design before testing on held-out masses, friction changes and sensor noise. Include scenarios that violate the assumed uncertainty model and explain the resulting failures.
evaluation: Report tracking, control effort and saturation.
Separate constant parameter error from time-varying disturbances.
Check whether parameter estimates converge under informative and uninformative motions.

sources.label: Doyle et al.: H2 and H-infinity synthesis
Dawson, Gao and Fan: learned certificates

chapters.title: Optimal control, MPC and trajectory optimization
chapters.subtitle: Choosing actions over time while respecting dynamics and constraints
chapters.question: What is the best feasible motion, and can it be recomputed before the next control deadline?
chapters.summary: Optimal control makes the design objective explicit: choose a policy or trajectory to minimize a cost while obeying dynamics and constraints. Its practical difficulty comes from long horizons, nonlinear motion, contact and uncertainty. The central distinctions are trajectory versus feedback, local versus global optimality, and numerical success versus physical feasibility.

sections.heading: A cost is a design decision
sections.text: A typical objective sums tracking error, effort, time or risk along a trajectory and adds a terminal cost. Constraints specify what is forbidden rather than merely expensive. A large collision penalty does not automatically enforce collision avoidance, because an optimizer can trade that penalty against other benefits. Units and scales also matter: changing a position unit without changing its weight changes the problem. Before comparing solvers, check that they are solving the same physically meaningful task.

sections.heading: Dynamic programming and trajectory optimization answer different questions
sections.text: Dynamic programming reasons about the best remaining cost from every relevant state. Bellman's principle links a decision now to the best continuation, yielding a feedback policy. Its state-space representation can become prohibitively large. Direct trajectory optimization instead searches for a sequence from a chosen initial state. Shooting optimizes inputs and simulates states; transcription optimizes states and inputs with dynamics constraints. A good open-loop solution still needs feedback to handle disturbances.

sections.heading: MPC turns repeated planning into feedback
sections.text: Model predictive control solves a finite-horizon problem, applies the first action, measures again and repeats. This makes constraints and changing conditions explicit. However, receding the horizon does not automatically prove stability or safety. Terminal ingredients, a feasible backup policy, uncertainty treatment and the solver's behavior all matter. Recursive feasibility means that solving today's problem leaves a feasible problem tomorrow under specified assumptions; it is stronger than observing that the optimizer succeeded on a few trajectories.

sections.heading: Convexity is valuable, but identify where it applies
sections.text: A convex subproblem can often be solved reliably, yet the original trajectory problem may remain nonconvex. Lossless convexification exploits special structure so a relaxed solution recovers an original solution under stated conditions. Successive convexification repeatedly builds local convex approximations, using mechanisms such as trust regions and virtual controls to manage linearization errors. Convergence results have assumptions and do not generally mean global optimality of every nonlinear mission. Check the final trajectory against the original dynamics and constraints.

sections.heading: Gradients, samples and contacts
sections.text: iLQR and differential dynamic programming exploit derivatives and local quadratic models. Sampling-based methods such as MPPI evaluate many rollouts and aggregate promising perturbations; parallel computation can make this useful when analytic derivatives are awkward. Finite samples still miss possibilities, and soft penalties need not enforce hard constraints. Contact introduces additional difficulty because touching, separating and impact change the dynamics. Complementarity formulations can search contact choices implicitly, at the cost of a challenging nonconvex optimization problem.

sections.heading: The research frontier is often in the interface
sections.text: Learned models, value functions and warm starts can reduce computation or improve generalization. Their role should be stated precisely: predicting a good initial guess differs from replacing the dynamics or directly outputting a control action. Evaluate wall-clock latency distributions, unsuccessful solves and constraint residuals, not just average objective value. A slightly worse plan that is reliably available in time may outperform an elegant solution delivered after the vehicle has moved.

open_questions: When does a learned warm start improve reliability rather than only median solve time?
How can contact and perception uncertainty be incorporated without exceeding the control deadline?
pitfalls: Calling each convex subproblem a globally optimal solution to the original nonconvex task.
Comparing objective values while hiding infeasible or timed-out trials.
Treating discretization nodes as proof of continuous-time constraint satisfaction.

project.title: Three ways to replan around an obstacle
project.description: Implement nonlinear MPC for a simple vehicle using a gradient solver and a rollout sampler, with a fixed safe fallback. Compare them under identical dynamics, observation noise and computation budgets. Add a learned warm start only after establishing both baselines.
evaluation: Measure end-to-end solve-time percentiles and deadline misses.
Validate continuous trajectories between optimization nodes.
Report success, effort, constraint violations and recovery from infeasible starts.

chapters.title: Reachability, barriers and formal methods
chapters.subtitle: Turning a desired behavior into a claim that can be checked
chapters.question: What exactly is guaranteed, for which states, disturbances, observations and implementations?
chapters.summary: Safety research begins by specifying an undesirable event or required behavior and identifying the assumptions under which it must be excluded. Different tools answer different questions: barriers preserve sets, reachability reasons over future possibilities, and formal synthesis enforces logical task structure. Learned systems make the interface between these layers especially important.

sections.heading: Specify the property before the method
sections.text: Avoiding an obstacle, eventually reaching a destination and remaining near an equilibrium are different properties. Safety excludes forbidden behavior; liveness requires progress; stability concerns how trajectories respond to perturbations. State whether a guarantee is deterministic, worst-case over a bounded disturbance set, or probabilistic under a distribution. Specify the initial set and time horizon. A collision-free training run is evidence about that run, not a statement covering every admissible initial condition.

sections.heading: Barrier functions enforce local conditions for set invariance
sections.text: A control barrier function encodes a safe set, often as h(x) ≥ 0. A derivative inequality constrains the input so the system cannot cross the boundary under the theorem's regularity and feasibility assumptions. A quadratic program can minimally modify a nominal command while enforcing that inequality. The difficult work is finding a valid barrier and ensuring an admissible input exists. Input saturation, higher relative degree, estimation error and discrete sampling all require treatment; they are not automatically covered by writing a QP.

sections.heading: Reachability asks which outcomes remain possible
sections.text: Hamilton–Jacobi reachability formulates safety as a dynamic game between control and disturbance. A value function characterizes states from which a target or failure set can be reached under chosen quantifiers. It can expose unavoidable failure and synthesize protective actions. Grid-based computation becomes costly as dimension increases, motivating decomposition and approximation. Every approximation should state whether it is conservative, optimistic or unverified; a visually plausible boundary is not enough to certify a safe region.

sections.heading: Logic connects low-level motion to mission intent
sections.text: Temporal logic can express sequences and persistent obligations: avoid a region, repeatedly visit locations, or respond to an event. Reactive synthesis constructs a strategy satisfying the specification against an explicitly modeled environment. The guarantee depends on the abstraction relating continuous motion to discrete states and on environmental assumptions. If those assumptions permit the environment to block every route, the task may be unrealizable. That diagnosis can be more useful than a controller that silently violates the mission.

sections.heading: Learning a certificate differs from verifying it
sections.text: Neural networks can propose Lyapunov, barrier or contraction certificates alongside a policy. Training losses encourage inequalities at sampled states; verification must establish what holds between samples and outside the training distribution. Counterexample-guided methods alternate learning and search for violations, while formal tools may prove restricted claims. Statistical approaches provide another kind of assurance: perception calibration can support probabilistic obstacle-avoidance claims without becoming a worst-case proof. Preserve that distinction when comparing papers.

sections.heading: System safety requires composition and monitoring
sections.text: A sound controller can fail when its state estimate is wrong, its safe set omits an obstacle, or its computation arrives late. Therefore list assumptions at every interface: perception error, model discrepancy, actuation and timing. Runtime assurance can monitor those assumptions and switch to a verified fallback, provided the switch remains possible early enough. Useful research measures intervention rate, conservatism and task completion as well as violations; a system that never moves can be safe yet accomplish nothing.

open_questions: How can guarantees compose across learned perception, planning and control without becoming unusably conservative?
Can high-dimensional safety approximations retain explicit error bounds at real-time rates?
pitfalls: Calling sampled certificate checks a proof over a continuous state space.
Ignoring infeasibility when several barrier constraints conflict.
Combining probabilistic modules without accounting for dependence or accumulated risk.

project.title: A nominal policy with an honest safety filter
project.description: Use a double-integrator robot approaching an obstacle. Compare an unconstrained controller, a barrier QP and a small-grid reachability controller. Add bounded model error and state-estimation error, then document exactly which implementation matches each method's assumptions.
evaluation: Plot feasible and infeasible initial-state regions.
Measure intervention, progress and constraint violations.
Stress sampling rate and actuator limits.
Separate empirical coverage from mathematically certified coverage.

sources.label: Kress-Gazit et al.: reactive temporal-logic planning
Dawson et al.: learned certificate survey
Mei et al.: statistical perception safety

chapters.title: Spacecraft and flight guidance, navigation and control
chapters.subtitle: Autonomy under orbital dynamics, limited actuation and mission constraints
chapters.question: How does a vehicle estimate its motion, choose a feasible maneuver and execute it with mission-level reliability?
chapters.summary: Guidance chooses where and how the vehicle should move, navigation estimates its state, and control produces the forces and torques needed to follow the plan. In spacecraft and aircraft these functions are tightly coupled by sensing, propulsion, geometry and deadlines. Space GNC is therefore a natural bridge from classical control to perception and autonomous decision-making.

sections.heading: Mission and dynamics determine the problem
sections.text: Attitude pointing, orbital transfer, formation flying, rendezvous, powered landing and atmospheric flight are distinct tasks. A model suitable for small relative motion near a reference orbit may fail during a large transfer or in a multi-body environment. Decide which gravitational perturbations, aerodynamic effects, flexible modes and actuator dynamics matter at the mission's scale. More fidelity is not always better: an onboard model must balance predictive accuracy with computation and the quantities actually constrained by the mission.

sections.heading: Attitude is geometry plus hardware
sections.text: A rigid body's orientation belongs to SO(3); position and orientation together can be represented on SE(3). Euler-angle singularities and quaternion conventions are representation issues with practical consequences. Geometric control works directly with the manifold, but almost-global results still have exceptions and actuator assumptions. Spacecraft reaction wheels store angular momentum and can saturate, requiring external torque for unloading. Thrusters and magnetic torquers have different authority and constraints, so a generic torque command is not a complete flight-control design.

sections.heading: Guidance is constrained optimization
sections.text: Powered descent and proximity operations must respect thrust magnitude, pointing, fuel, terrain, keep-out regions and terminal conditions. Convexification methods make selected problem classes or local approximations tractable for repeated solution. A relaxation can be lossless only under particular conditions; a sequence of convex solves does not automatically make the original mission globally optimal. Check discretization error, original-model feasibility and the availability of an abort or backup trajectory when navigation updates change the problem.

sections.heading: Navigation can become the limiting subsystem
sections.text: A cooperative spacecraft may provide navigation aids; an uncooperative target may require pose inference from images under severe illumination and viewpoint changes. Learned pose estimation can initialize or support a geometric estimator, but synthetic training data introduce a domain gap. Distinguish detecting a target, estimating its relative pose and estimating its motion over time. A useful navigation objective also considers uncertainty and observability: a short path that loses the target can be worse than a longer, informative approach.

sections.heading: Flight robotics shares methods, not every assumption
sections.text: Quadrotors, landing rockets and free-flying spacecraft all motivate geometric models, trajectory tracking and limited-input control. Their disturbance environments differ: aerodynamic forces and fast motor response dominate many small-aircraft experiments, while orbit dynamics, propellant budgets and long communication delays shape spacecraft operations. Transfer an algorithm by rebuilding its assumptions and evaluation, not by changing a simulator's vehicle mesh. This is where estimation, robust control and computational guidance become a coherent research program.

sections.heading: Read the evidence at mission level
sections.text: Separate numerical trajectories, Monte Carlo simulations, processor-in-the-loop timing, hardware-in-the-loop tests, free-flight experiments and actual mission operation. Each answers a different question; none automatically validates every subsystem. A publication may demonstrate a planning solver while assuming perfect navigation, or a pose network while never closing the control loop. Strong application research states those boundaries and tests failure modes, recovery behavior and uncertainty. For graduate fit, identify which layer a laboratory actually develops and validates.

open_questions: How can perception uncertainty enter onboard guidance without making every maneuver infeasible?
What evidence is sufficient to trust learned warm starts or learned dynamics during rare mission-critical events?
pitfalls: Treating a pose-estimation benchmark as autonomous rendezvous validation.
Comparing guidance algorithms under inconsistent propulsion or navigation assumptions.
Transferring a local relative-orbit model to a regime where its approximation is invalid.

project.title: Closed-loop rendezvous with uncertain navigation
project.description: Start with planar relative motion and bounded thrust. Couple a noisy relative-position estimator to receding-horizon guidance with a keep-out region and a feasible retreat policy. Then deliberately degrade the model and measurements; add full three-dimensional attitude only after the simpler closed loop is understood.
evaluation: Report propellant proxy, terminal error and keep-out violations.
Measure estimator uncertainty and guidance feasibility together.
Include delay, dropout and actuator saturation.
Label simulation evidence explicitly and avoid flight claims.

sources.label: Sullivan et al.: relative-motion model survey
Lee, Leok and McClamroch: geometric flight control
Malyuta et al.: convex trajectory-generation tutorial
Sharma et al.: spacecraft pose estimation

chapters.title: Motion and task planning
chapters.subtitle: From a desired outcome to a feasible sequence of movements
chapters.question: How can a robot choose actions that reach a goal while respecting geometry, dynamics, and task constraints?
chapters.summary: Planning connects a task such as putting a cup in a cupboard to concrete movements. It is not one algorithm: choosing which objects to move, finding collision-free configurations, timing a trajectory, and repairing a failed action are different problems. A useful starting point is to ask what the planner treats as known, which decisions it controls, and whether its output can actually be followed by the robot.

sections.heading: Choose the right mathematical object
sections.text: A configuration describes the robot's shape or pose; a state also includes variables such as velocity that influence its future. A geometric path is an untimed curve through configurations. A trajectory adds time, and a feedback policy specifies what to do as observations change. An arm can have a collision-free path that violates acceleration limits when timed too aggressively. A car cannot follow every curve that fits between obstacles because steering and forward motion impose constraints. Define the state, controls, collision model, goal conditions, and cost before selecting a solver. These choices often matter more than the algorithm's name.

sections.heading: Sampling and optimization solve different difficulties
sections.text: Sampling methods search a continuous space by building a graph or tree from sampled states. RRT* and FMT* explain how solution quality can improve with increasing computation under specified assumptions. Their asymptotic guarantees do not promise a good answer within a particular control deadline. Trajectory optimization instead improves a candidate motion using costs and constraints; CHOMP and TrajOpt are useful entry points. Optimization can exploit smooth structure efficiently, but initialization and local minima matter. Narrow passages challenge sampling, while competing routes around an obstacle challenge local optimization. A practical combination searches for distinct route candidates, then optimizes and validates each feasible trajectory.

sections.heading: Task decisions change the motion problem
sections.text: Opening a cupboard, moving a blocking object, and choosing a grasp alter which motions are possible. Task and motion planning couples discrete decisions with continuous geometry. PDDLStream illustrates an architecture in which symbolic planning calls specialized samplers for grasps, placements, or other continuous choices. The symbolic model must represent relevant preconditions and effects: a plan that assumes a door is open cannot repair an omitted door-opening skill by reasoning harder. Distinguish a task-level action from a reliable controller implementing it. Contact, deformable objects, uncertain friction, and ambiguous object identities make that interface substantially harder than rigid-body collision checking.

sections.heading: The planner lives inside an execution loop
sections.text: A plan is conditional on a model and observations. Replanning updates an open-loop proposal when estimates or obstacles change; feedback control handles faster deviations. Under partial observability, the planner may need to reason about a belief over states and choose informative actions. Looking around a corner can be valuable even when it initially increases distance to the goal. Receding-horizon execution helps manage change but can become shortsighted or oscillatory. Define the behavior when no feasible plan is found, how stale trajectories are detected, and how execution success is checked. Planner feasibility is not a universal safety guarantee for the complete sensing and control system.

open_questions: How can planners trade exploration, task progress, and risk under uncertain geometry?
How should a planner recognize that its skill library or symbolic model cannot express the task?
Which combinations of learned proposals and explicit search retain useful reliability guarantees?
pitfalls: Confusing geometric collision freedom with dynamically feasible or safe execution.
Reporting only successful runs or mean planning time, which hides deadline failures.
Treating asymptotic optimality as a finite-time guarantee or assuming a local optimum is globally best.

project.title: One task, three planning representations
project.description: Build a small simulated mobile manipulator task with two routes and an object blocking one route. Compare a sampling planner, trajectory optimization initialized from a route, and a task planner allowed to move the obstruction. Keep geometry and execution limits identical.
evaluation: Record success and timeout rates over fixed randomized start-goal pairs, including infeasible instances.
Report path cost, execution time, minimum clearance, and median plus upper-tail computation time.
Perturb object positions during execution and measure recovery rather than silently restarting failed trials.

sources.label: LaValle, Planning Algorithms: configuration spaces, search, differential constraints, and uncertainty
Karaman and Frazzoli: asymptotically optimal sampling-based planning

chapters.title: SLAM, mapping, and spatial intelligence
chapters.subtitle: Estimating where the robot is while building a usable account of its surroundings
chapters.question: How can a robot construct a consistent world model from noisy observations while moving through that same world?
chapters.summary: Simultaneous localization and mapping, or SLAM, couples two unknowns: robot motion and environmental structure. Knowing the map helps estimate motion, while knowing motion helps assemble the map. Spatial intelligence adds questions about objects, relationships, and how the world changes. The central research problem is not simply producing an attractive reconstruction; it is maintaining a trustworthy representation that supports navigation, interaction, and recovery.

sections.heading: Geometry is inferred, not directly given
sections.text: A camera measures image intensity, not world coordinates. Inferring depth and motion requires assumptions, multiple views, additional sensors, or learned information. Monocular geometry has an unresolved scale without further information; arbitrary global position and orientation can also remain unobservable. An inertial sensor supplies motion information but introduces biases, calibration parameters, and drift. VINS-Mono is a useful route into visual-inertial estimation. Calibration, time synchronization, and sufficiently informative movement are part of the estimation problem. A stationary or poorly excited sensor suite cannot reveal every unknown merely because an optimizer has more iterations.

sections.heading: Association and estimation form a fragile partnership
sections.text: A typical system extracts observations, associates them with previously seen structure, and optimizes a graph of states and measurements. The front end proposes correspondences; the back end reconciles their constraints. Loop closure recognizes a revisited place and can correct accumulated drift, but a false loop closure can damage an otherwise good map. Robust losses help with some outliers but do not make arbitrary false associations harmless. ORB-SLAM3 provides a feature-based visual and visual-inertial reference, while DROID-SLAM shows how learned components can be combined with geometric optimization. Compare their assumptions, operating conditions, and failure recovery rather than reducing the distinction to classical versus neural.

sections.heading: Choose a map for the decision it must support
sections.text: A sparse landmark map may be enough for localization, an occupancy or distance map for collision avoidance, and a dense surface model for inspection. Semantic maps attach object or category information; scene graphs represent relationships such as containment or support. Kimera makes metric-semantic mapping concrete, while ConceptGraphs explores open-vocabulary object-centric structure. These representations are complementary rather than a single ladder of progress. A visually convincing rendering need not provide conservative collision geometry, and a semantic label need not identify an object instance consistently across time. Ask what uncertainties the map preserves, which updates it permits, and how a downstream planner consumes it.

sections.heading: Evaluate consistency, persistence, and task consequences
sections.text: Real environments contain moving people, rearranged furniture, seasonal changes, repeated textures, and long periods without useful features. A system must decide what belongs to a persistent map and what should be treated as temporary. Global trajectory error summarizes one aspect of performance, but alignment can hide some gauge ambiguities and it says little about local obstacle accuracy. Include relative motion error, tracking losses, relocalization, map consistency, latency, and memory growth. A robot should also know when its localization has become unreliable. For applications, the decisive test is often whether mapping errors cause a navigation or manipulation failure, not which trajectory plot looks smoothest.

open_questions: How can a robot maintain maps across months while separating persistent structure from temporary changes?
What uncertainty representation remains useful when geometry and semantic predictions come from learned models?
How can multi-session mapping detect confidently wrong correspondences before they corrupt the shared map?
pitfalls: Equating a good rendering with an accurate or collision-safe map.
Comparing trajectories without stating alignment, scale treatment, sensor inputs, and failures.
Treating semantic categories as stable object identities or silently discarding tracking-loss episodes.

project.title: A map that survives a changed room
project.description: Replay the same indoor route before and after moving several objects. Compare a localization-focused map with an object-aware map, then inspect whether the changed objects damage relocalization or planning.
evaluation: State the trajectory alignment method and report absolute plus relative pose errors.
Count tracking losses, incorrect loop closures, and time required to relocalize.
Measure obstacle-map errors near the robot's route, memory growth, and navigation success after rearrangement.

sources.label: Cadena and colleagues: Past, Present, and Future of SLAM

chapters.title: 3D and multimodal robot perception
chapters.subtitle: Turning sensor measurements into information that can guide action
chapters.question: Which representation of the world lets a robot act reliably, and what evidence supports that representation?
chapters.summary: Robot perception estimates properties that matter for action: where surfaces are, which objects are present, how they move, and which interactions might succeed. Recognition is only part of the job. A robot also needs calibrated geometry, timing, uncertainty, and an understanding of what it has not observed. The right representation depends on the action: recognizing a cup, grasping its handle, and pouring from it demand different information.

sections.heading: Start from the sensing contract
sections.text: An image provides rich appearance but does not directly resolve depth or physical properties. Depth cameras and lidar provide geometric measurements with their own range limits and failure conditions; tactile sensing reveals contact where vision may be occluded. Combining sensors requires coordinate calibration and time synchronization, not merely concatenating features. A fast robot can act on a badly outdated scene even when each individual prediction is accurate. Specify what each measurement means, when it was captured, and which surfaces or motions it cannot resolve. Sensor placement and active camera movement can improve information before any new neural architecture is introduced.

sections.heading: Representation determines what the learner can express
sections.text: Point clouds, voxels, meshes, implicit fields, and images preserve different structures and create different computational costs. PointNet is a foundational example of processing unordered point sets while respecting permutation invariance. That property is different from invariance or equivariance to rotations and translations. A model may classify an object correctly while estimating its pose poorly. Dense radiance representations, including 3D Gaussian splatting, optimize a rendering objective; their success at producing images does not automatically certify surfaces for contact or collision checks. Decide whether a representation is serving localization, novel-view synthesis, manipulation, or several tasks, and test each claim separately.

sections.heading: Language expands labels but does not remove grounding
sections.text: Vision-language models such as CLIP make it possible to connect images to a broader range of textual concepts than a small fixed label set. A textual match is not a verified object identity, a physical affordance, or a feasible instruction. Open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs, exemplified by ConceptGraphs, combine observed geometry with semantic descriptions and relationships. Distinguish measured spatial relationships from inferred functional ones: an object near a table is not necessarily supported by it. Ambiguous descriptions, unusual viewpoints, occlusion, and repeated objects can break these links. A useful system can revise an interpretation after new observations rather than treating the first semantic prediction as permanent truth.

sections.heading: Assess perception through closed-loop consequences
sections.text: Benchmark accuracy and segmentation overlap help isolate components, but they do not fully characterize a robot's behavior. A small error at a grasp contact can matter more than a large background error. Evaluate calibration, confidence, latency, and failure detection alongside task success. Test novel objects, lighting changes, clutter, transparent or reflective surfaces, and partial views when relevant to the application. Active perception chooses a movement to reduce uncertainty, creating a direct connection to planning and estimation. The research question becomes which information is worth acquiring before acting, and when the robot should proceed despite uncertainty instead of waiting for an impossible complete reconstruction.

open_questions: How should geometric and semantic uncertainty be represented together for downstream action?
When does tactile or active visual sensing provide more benefit than a larger passive perception model?
How can open-vocabulary systems identify unknown or contradictory evidence instead of assigning a plausible label?
pitfalls: Assuming language similarity establishes an object's identity or physical affordance.
Treating permutation invariance as rotation invariance.
Claiming robot readiness from offline recognition metrics without measuring calibration, latency, and action failures.

project.title: Does the representation help the grasp?
project.description: Build an object selection and grasping benchmark in simulation or on an existing safe tabletop platform. Compare fixed-label detection, text-conditioned selection, and a geometry-aware object representation using the same grasp controller.
evaluation: Separate object-selection errors, pose errors, unreachable grasps, and execution failures.
Hold out object instances and descriptions, and vary clutter plus viewpoint.
Measure end-to-end latency and test whether one additional camera view improves success more than increasing model size.

chapters.title: Aerial and field autonomy
chapters.subtitle: Connecting perception, planning, and control under real physical limits
chapters.question: How can an autonomous robot keep making useful progress when sensing is incomplete, dynamics are fast, and conditions change?
chapters.summary: Field autonomy studies robots operating beyond a fixed, tightly controlled workspace. Drones make the central issues especially visible: motion changes observations, computation takes time, and an error can become unrecoverable before another plan is ready. Ground, marine, agricultural, and inspection robots face related problems with different dynamics and sensing conditions. The research challenge is to integrate estimation, decision making, and control so that their assumptions remain compatible during execution.

sections.heading: The sensing horizon limits the maneuver
sections.text: A planner cannot safely exploit agility that the sensing and estimation system cannot support. For an idealized one-dimensional stop with constant available deceleration a, braking distance grows as v squared divided by 2a; sensing and computation delay add distance traveled before braking begins. This is an intuition, not a complete drone safety model: orientation limits, actuator saturation, wind, and three-dimensional maneuvers also matter. An occluded obstacle may enter view too late for any controller to avoid it. Analyze the full chain from exposure time through estimation and planning to actuator response, and choose speed or margins that reflect its uncertainty.

sections.heading: Model-based and learned decisions can be combined
sections.text: Model-based methods construct trajectories subject to geometric and dynamic constraints and update them as the local map changes. Topology-guided UAV replanning illustrates why considering distinct routes can help an optimizer avoid poor local choices. Learned policies can compress difficult inference or planning computations into a fast decision rule, but their behavior depends on training coverage. Learning high-speed flight in the wild demonstrates a route from privileged training information to onboard visual decisions. Neither approach eliminates estimation, calibration, or low-level control requirements. Hybrid systems can use learning to propose motions while checking or refining them with explicit constraints, at the cost of extra computation and interface design.

sections.heading: Match the evidence to the claimed capability
sections.text: Champion-level drone racing demonstrates a demanding but structured task: rapid flight through a known racing course, with task-specific training and a deployed perception-control system. It should not be read as evidence for arbitrary outdoor exploration or recovery from every disturbance. Conversely, a method that navigates unfamiliar obstacles may not optimize racing time or aggressive flight at the same level. Compare what is known before deployment, what information is available during training, and what is observed online. The same distinction applies to a field robot following crop rows versus one exploring unknown terrain. Task definitions make impressive results interpretable.

sections.heading: Recovery and operating conditions are part of the system
sections.text: Wind, changing light, rain, vegetation, moving obstacles, wheel slip, or sensor degradation can invalidate different parts of a pipeline. Some failures call for slower motion, a new view, relocalization, or a different route; others require ending the mission. Define these modes and the conditions for switching between them rather than hiding them in manual intervention. Evaluate closed-loop performance across stated operating conditions, including failures and aborted attempts. Report mission completion, collisions or contacts, state-estimation losses, intervention frequency, energy, latency, and recovery time where relevant. A reliable field system needs evidence about the boundaries of operation as well as a convincing successful demonstration.

open_questions: How can operating limits be estimated online when sensing, dynamics, and environment shift together?
Which failures can a robot recover from using its existing sensors and skills?
How should field experiments compare systems with different amounts of prior mapping and training information?
pitfalls: Calling a known-course racing result general navigation without stating the task differences.
Measuring planning speed while ignoring image acquisition, estimation, communication, and actuator latency.
Treating a safety check's model assumptions as guaranteed properties of the physical environment.

project.title: A speed-versus-visibility autonomy study
project.description: In simulation, fly or drive the same route with controlled sensor range, delay, and disturbance levels. Compare a fixed-speed policy with one that adjusts speed to visibility and estimated uncertainty.
evaluation: Report completion, collisions, interventions, and travel time across all runs.
Sweep sensing range and total delay separately to identify which bottleneck controls performance.
Test a held-out obstacle arrangement and report whether recovery succeeds after an estimation interruption.

sources.label: Learning high-speed flight in the wild, Science Robotics 2021
Champion-level drone racing using deep reinforcement learning, Nature 2023

chapters.title: Multi-robot and distributed systems
chapters.subtitle: Coordinating many decision makers with limited information
chapters.question: How can a team coordinate motion and tasks when each robot sees only part of the world and communication is constrained?
chapters.summary: Adding robots creates opportunities for coverage, transport, exploration, and resilience, but also creates new coupling. Robots compete for space, exchange uncertain information, and may disagree about the state of the world. Multi-robot research asks which decisions should be centralized, which can be made locally, and what information must move between agents. A team can be individually competent yet collectively inefficient, deadlocked, or unsafe.

sections.heading: Separate the coordination problem from the architecture
sections.text: Task allocation assigns responsibilities; path planning avoids conflicts; formation control maintains relationships; consensus drives agents toward agreement on a quantity. Solving one does not solve the others. A centralized system makes decisions using a shared view, while a decentralized controller acts from local information; distributed computation can involve substantial message exchange without a single central decision maker. Centralization can simplify global reasoning but creates communication and scaling costs. Local policies respond quickly but may lack the information needed to resolve a bottleneck. State the communication model and information available to each agent before comparing algorithms or claiming decentralization.

sections.heading: Graphs describe who can influence whom
sections.text: In consensus and coordination, a graph represents sensing or communication relationships. Its connectivity affects whether information can propagate across the team; delays, changing links, and directed communication alter the analysis. Consensus theory supplies precise results under explicit assumptions, but agreeing on a number is not equivalent to completing a shared task or avoiding collisions. Geometry adds another graph: two robots may interfere physically even when they cannot communicate. A third graph may describe task dependencies. Keeping these relationships distinct helps reveal hidden assumptions, such as treating every nearby robot as immediately observable with an accurate synchronized state.

sections.heading: Learning can use structure without removing constraints
sections.text: Graph neural networks share computation across agents and aggregate neighbor information, making them a natural architecture for variable-sized teams. Work on learned swarm controllers and decentralized path planning shows how local policies can be trained from stronger information or demonstrations. Permutation symmetry helps avoid dependence on arbitrary agent numbering; it does not guarantee generalization to any team size, density, map, or communication range. GLAS illustrates combining learned motion decisions with a separate safety mechanism. Always inspect what the safety component assumes, whether it changes the learned action, and whether collision avoidance comes at the cost of stalled progress or oscillation.

sections.heading: Measure team behavior, including communication and recovery
sections.text: The joint planning space grows rapidly with team size, but robot count alone is a poor measure of difficulty. Ten robots in a narrow corridor can be harder than hundreds in open space. Vary density, obstacle structure, assignment difficulty, sensing range, delay, and packet loss. Report completion, collisions, makespan, total path cost, fairness or starvation, and messages or bytes exchanged. Distinguish decentralized execution from centralized training and from a central service used at test time. Include robot failures and changing membership when those are part of the claim. The strongest evidence explains which information enables coordination and what fails when that information is removed.

open_questions: What minimal information allows local controllers to resolve bottlenecks without deadlock?
How can formal guarantees survive changing communication graphs and imperfect state estimates?
When does learned coordination transfer across team sizes, robot capabilities, and task distributions?
pitfalls: Claiming decentralized execution while using a global planner or shared ground-truth state at deployment.
Equating collision avoidance with successful coordinated progress.
Testing only robot count while keeping density and communication difficulty artificially easy.

project.title: The corridor stress test
project.description: Compare centralized planning, a local collision-avoidance baseline, and a learned or rule-based neighbor policy on shared-goal and opposing-flow tasks. Use the same dynamics and information budget wherever the comparison permits.
evaluation: Sweep corridor width, team density, communication range, and delay.
Report deadlocks, collisions, completion, makespan, and per-agent waiting time.
Ablate messages and introduce one stopped robot to test recovery and dependence on central information.

sources.label: Olfati-Saber, Fax, and Murray: consensus and cooperation
Learning Decentralized Controllers for Robot Swarms with Graph Neural Networks
GLAS: learned multi-robot motion planning with a safety mechanism
Graph Neural Networks for Decentralized Multi-Robot Path Planning
LaValle: search and multi-robot planning foundations

chapters.title: Embodied AI and task reasoning
chapters.subtitle: Grounding language and general knowledge in what a robot can observe and do
chapters.question: How can a robot turn an open-ended instruction into verifiable progress in a physical environment?
chapters.summary: Embodied AI links perception, memory, task reasoning, and action. A request such as putting away the cup requires resolving which cup, locating a suitable destination, selecting skills, checking physical feasibility, and recognizing completion. Language models broaden the range of instructions a system can interpret, but fluency does not establish that a plan is executable. The central issue is grounding: connecting symbols and predictions to observations, capabilities, and consequences.

sections.heading: Understand the interfaces before comparing models
sections.text: There are several useful integration points. A language model can propose a task plan, choose among existing skills, process sensory information, or participate in producing action commands. These are different capabilities. SayCan combines linguistic relevance with estimates of what available skills can accomplish. PaLM-E incorporates continuous sensory representations into an embodied language-model architecture. RT-2 studies vision-language-action models that connect visual and language inputs to robot actions. OpenVLA provides an open model and adaptation route for investigating such systems. Ask what each model outputs and which other components still perform perception, motion planning, feedback control, and success detection.

sections.heading: World models and task models make assumptions explicit
sections.text: A task planner benefits from a representation of objects, locations, relations, and skill preconditions. SayPlan uses hierarchical 3D scene graphs and feedback from a graph-based simulator to organize task planning. PDDLStream instead connects symbolic planning to continuous samplers, illustrating a different way to expose geometric feasibility. Both make parts of the decision process inspectable, but neither representation automatically captures every physical consequence. An object described as inside a cupboard may be occluded, unreachable, or attached to something else. The system must distinguish observed facts, inferred relations, and uncertain beliefs, and update them when execution contradicts the plan.

sections.heading: Modularity and end-to-end learning have different costs
sections.text: A modular system permits focused debugging: an incorrect object association differs from a failed grasp or an invalid task precondition. Its interfaces can also discard information and require substantial engineering. A model trained to predict actions can capture correlations that are hard to encode manually, but diagnosis and transfer across robots become more difficult. Robot-action data, embodiment, control frequency, and action representation matter; language pretraining alone does not supply an arbitrary missing physical skill. Hybrid designs can combine learned skill proposals with explicit state checks and motion constraints. Evaluate whether each extra component improves reliability enough to justify its latency, data requirements, and failure modes.

sections.heading: Reasoning must be evaluated through completed episodes
sections.text: A plausible verbal plan is an intermediate output, not the final objective. Measure whether the robot completes the requested task, recognizes failure, and recovers without unreported assistance. Separate generalization to new objects, layouts, language descriptions, skill combinations, and embodiments. A task containing familiar subskills in a new order tests something different from a task requiring an unseen manipulation capability. Report the training and adaptation budget, allowed retries, reset conditions, and human interventions. For long tasks, even moderately reliable skills can compound into poor overall completion. Useful research identifies the source of improvement: better perception, better skill selection, stronger execution, or better recovery.

open_questions: How can a robot detect that an instruction requires a capability absent from its current skill repertoire?
Which memory and world representations support long tasks without accumulating confidently wrong beliefs?
How can evaluations distinguish compositional generalization from overlap with training or adaptation data?
pitfalls: Using a well-written plan as evidence of successful physical execution.
Attributing an entire system's performance to its language model without checking controllers, demonstrations, or human resets.
Treating unseen wording, unseen objects, unseen skills, and unseen embodiments as the same generalization claim.

project.title: Grounded instruction following with failure feedback
project.description: Build a small simulated kitchen or tabletop world with a fixed skill library. Compare language-only skill selection with selection grounded in observable preconditions and execution feedback. Include impossible requests and tasks where one skill deliberately fails.
evaluation: Measure full-episode success, incorrect success declarations, unnecessary actions, and interventions.
Separate paraphrase tests from new object arrangements and new skill compositions.
Track whether the agent detects missing capabilities and recovers from a failed action without silently resetting the scene.

chapters.title: Reinforcement learning for control
chapters.subtitle: Learning feedback decisions from consequences
chapters.question: When is learning a controller from interaction preferable to designing or optimizing one directly?
chapters.summary: Reinforcement learning is a way to choose behavior from consequences over time. In robotics, its output is often a feedback policy inside a larger control stack. A useful research question identifies which difficult component is learned, what information reaches that component, and what physical budget pays for its experience. Start with the control problem before choosing a neural-network architecture.

sections.heading: From a control problem to an objective
sections.text: Describe observations, actions, dynamics, a reward and a stopping rule. A typical objective is the expected discounted sum of rewards, E[∑ₜ γᵗ rₜ]. The policy chooses an action from observations or their history. The critic estimates future return. This formulation does not make the chosen reward correct: rewarding forward speed can encourage damaging impacts unless other requirements are represented. A reward penalty and a hard physical constraint have different meanings. Ask separately what the robot should achieve and what it must never exceed.

sections.heading: PPO, SAC and the price of experience
sections.text: PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) uses batches collected under a recent policy and limits changes through a surrogate objective. SAC (Haarnoja et al., 2018) reuses replayed transitions and adds entropy to its objective. These choices affect stability, exploration and data efficiency. A simulator can provide many cheap parallel rollouts, making on-policy methods attractive; a physical robot may make each interaction expensive. Compare environment interactions, training computation, reset labor and hyperparameter search separately. Faster gradient updates do not necessarily mean cheaper research.

sections.heading: Learning and optimization can share a system
sections.text: A model-based method learns or uses dynamics; a model-free method learns behavior or values without requiring an explicit transition model for its updates. Neither category means the complete robot lacks a model. Guided policy search connects local trajectory optimization with global policy fitting (Levine et al., 2016). An RL policy may output desired joint positions to a conventional servo, tune an MPC cost, or provide a residual correction. This creates concrete comparisons: which model error is learned away, and which controller already supplies stability?

sections.heading: Observation history, deployment and failure
