sections.text: A simulator may expose friction, contact state or terrain geometry that deployment cannot measure. Such privileged information can help train a critic or teacher, but the deployed policy must have an achievable information path. Recurrence can summarize recent observations, yet it does not guarantee an identifiable or calibrated estimate. Examine delays, saturation and resets as part of the policy’s environment. A controller that succeeds only after frequent manual intervention has a different capability from one that recovers autonomously under the same disturbance distribution.

sections.heading: A tractable research direction
sections.text: Choose one mismatch and measure it. Examples include uncertain actuator delay, sparse rewards for assembly, or policy adaptation under changing payload. Keep a simple controller and one established learning method as baselines. Change one major assumption at a time, report distributions across training runs, and include failure examples. Youngwoon Lee’s stated interests in scalable reinforcement learning, humanoid control and dexterous manipulation sit at this intersection; his lab is one entry point into a much broader community, not a definition of the whole field.

open_questions: How can reward design express task success without making undesirable shortcuts easier?
When does online adaptation justify its interaction cost compared with robust offline training?
Which learned components admit useful safety or stability guarantees?
pitfalls: Treating reward optimization as proof that the physical task is solved.
Comparing methods with different observation access or reset budgets.
Calling a low-level position command direct torque control.

project.title: Delay-robust pendulum control
project.description: Compare a conventional feedback controller and one RL policy on a simulated pendulum while varying sensor delay and actuator limits. Preserve a held-out set of delay conditions.
evaluation: Tracking error and time within a target region.
Constraint violations and recovery after perturbations.
Interaction count, training seeds and performance outside training conditions.

chapters.title: Imitation, diffusion and vision-language-action policies
chapters.subtitle: From demonstration data to closed-loop skill
chapters.question: What does a policy learn from demonstrations, and what remains missing when it encounters an unfamiliar situation?
chapters.summary: Imitation learning starts with examples of behavior rather than requiring a reward to discover everything from scratch. The central question is not merely whether a model predicts recorded actions. It is whether those predictions keep the robot in situations where its knowledge remains useful. Modern sequence models and vision-language-action models change policy expressiveness and prior knowledge; they do not remove this closed-loop problem.

sections.heading: Behavior cloning and the distribution it never sees
sections.text: Behavior cloning fits actions from observations using supervised learning. It is an essential baseline because it is simple and can be effective with appropriate demonstrations. But a small action error changes the next observation; eventually the robot may visit states absent from its dataset. DAgger (Ross et al., 2011) tackles this by gathering expert labels along learner-induced trajectories. Its lesson extends beyond one algorithm: recovery examples and deployment-state coverage can matter more than reducing error on familiar frames.

sections.heading: Why predict a sequence or a distribution?
sections.text: An object can often be reached by several valid paths. Regressing their average may produce an invalid movement. Diffusion Policy represents a conditional distribution over action sequences; ACT predicts action chunks using a transformer-based approach. Both make temporal structure explicit, but the execution horizon still trades smoothness and computation against responsiveness. Predicting twenty actions does not require blindly executing twenty actions. The correct comparison includes when new sensor information enters, how latency is handled, and what happens when contact occurs earlier than expected.

sections.heading: Where language and pretraining enter
sections.text: RT-2 connects a pretrained vision-language model to robot action tokens. OpenVLA makes a related approach available with open weights and adaptation tools, while Octo studies flexible generalist-policy interfaces. Distinguish three abilities: recognizing a novel description, choosing the appropriate task, and physically executing it. Semantic transfer may improve the first two without supplying a missing contact skill. A language command also leaves details unspecified: which grasp, how much force, when to stop, and what counts as a recoverable mistake?

sections.heading: The dataset is part of the method
sections.text: Demonstrations encode camera placement, control frequency, action coordinates and the operator’s skill. A Cartesian displacement, joint target and torque are not interchangeable labels. Open X-Embodiment makes cross-robot data sharing a research problem through standardization and joint training. Robomimic shows why data quality, algorithm design and checkpoint selection need explicit study. Before fine-tuning a large model, inspect a small batch of trajectories, verify units and timestamps, and establish a baseline on exactly the same data. Dataset volume alone cannot establish useful coverage.

sections.heading: Choosing a research contribution
sections.text: A specialist imitation model can be a strong choice for a narrow precision task; a pretrained policy may offer better transfer across varied semantics or setups. Treat this as an empirical tradeoff, not a universal progression from small to large. Good projects isolate a bottleneck: recovery supervision, tactile conditioning, efficient adaptation, action-frequency changes or data filtering. Measure both familiar-task competence and the particular held-out variation you intend to improve. State how much target data is used; adaptation and zero-shot deployment answer different questions.

open_questions: How can a policy recognize that its demonstrations do not support the current state?
Which action representations transfer across embodiments without erasing physical meaning?
How much of a foundation policy’s benefit comes from representation rather than data coverage?
pitfalls: Evaluating only action prediction error.
Using the test environments to choose checkpoints or data mixtures.
Equating language fluency with physical reliability.

project.title: Recovery data versus a larger policy
project.description: Use a small simulated manipulation task to compare a compact cloning baseline with and without demonstrations of recovery from perturbed states. Keep the original demonstration and compute budgets visible.
evaluation: Closed-loop success on fixed initial-state splits.
Success after a controlled mid-episode disturbance.
Performance versus number and type of additional demonstrations.

sources.label: Diffusion Policy: original project and conference citation

chapters.title: Dexterity and contact-rich manipulation
chapters.subtitle: Controlling interaction, not just moving through space
chapters.question: Why can a robot reach an object accurately yet still fail to insert, rotate, assemble or use it?
chapters.summary: Manipulation changes the world through contact. Free-space reaching is only the approach: successful insertion or in-hand rotation depends on force, geometry, uncertainty and changing contact relationships. The field connects mechanical design, tactile sensing, planning, feedback control and learning. A useful graduate research problem often lives at one of these interfaces rather than belonging exclusively to an algorithm family.

sections.heading: The contact mode changes the problem
sections.text: A hand and object can separate, stick, slide, roll or collide. Each mode changes which motions and forces are possible. Friction constrains tangential forces relative to normal loading, and unilateral contact permits pushing but not pulling through an ordinary contact surface. The familiar smooth-dynamics picture becomes a piecewise problem with switches and uncertainty. Geometric accuracy alone may not reveal whether a peg is jammed. The manipulation course notes by Tedrake provide a physical starting point through contact frames, friction cones and grasp mechanics.

sections.heading: Different forms of dexterity
sections.text: A parallel gripper can achieve useful dexterity by pushing against the table, regrasping or using a fixture. A multi-finger hand offers more contact choices but also more states, actuators and sensing challenges. Bimanual manipulation adds coordination and shared loads; it is not automatically the same as in-hand dexterity. Choose a task-level requirement first: maintaining a stable grasp, moving an object within the fingers, inserting under uncertainty, or manipulating a deformable object. Hardware should support the experiment’s hypothesis rather than serve as its only novelty.

sections.heading: Models, local feedback and learned skill
sections.text: Model-based approaches expose geometry, constraints and forces to optimization, making some failures interpretable. They can struggle with uncertain contact parameters and combinatorial mode changes. Guided policy search demonstrated a route from learned local models to contact-intensive skills. Learning can absorb complicated interactions from experience, but its coverage and observation assumptions remain critical. A practical hybrid may use a planner for approach, a compliant controller for contact, and a learned policy for local adaptation. Compare the full stack and identify the component producing the improvement.

sections.heading: What demonstrations and simulation provide
sections.text: ACT and Diffusion Policy show how demonstration learning can capture temporally structured manipulation. OpenAI’s dexterous-hand work demonstrates simulated training transferred to real object reorientation. These are different evidence types: supervised behavior coverage versus exploration in a randomized model. Neither implies arbitrary dexterity. For real contact, force and tactile observations can reveal slip or loading that images miss; they also introduce calibration and synchronization problems. Treat the sensor interface and contact-event timing as part of the scientific method, not minor implementation details.

sections.heading: Long horizons expose hidden assumptions
sections.text: FurnitureBench, coauthored by Youngwoon Lee, makes assembly a reproducible test of perception, control and sequencing. If every stage succeeds with probability p and stages fail independently, a chain of n stages succeeds with probability p^n; real failures may be correlated, so this is an explanatory model rather than a measured law. It shows why strong individual skills can still produce weak full-task performance. Research opportunities include detecting incomplete insertions, choosing recovery actions, preserving useful intermediate states and deciding when another attempt risks making the task harder.

open_questions: How should tactile and visual signals be combined around contact transitions?
When is a fixture or tool a better solution than a more complex hand?
How can long-horizon policies detect and recover from partially successful actions?
pitfalls: Reporting reach accuracy as evidence of contact competence.
Conflating in-hand rotation with general dexterity.
Counting manually repaired partial executions as autonomous full-task successes.

project.title: Insertion under uncertainty
project.description: Simulate a peg-in-hole task and compare a position-only strategy with compliant local feedback under controlled pose and friction changes. Add a learned component only after diagnosing a repeatable failure.
evaluation: Success across an explicit pose-error grid.
Peak contact force, duration and failure categories.
Recovery success after a failed initial approach.

sources.label: Contact mechanics and manipulation: MIT course notes
Contact-rich guided policy search: author paper

chapters.title: Legged and humanoid control
chapters.subtitle: Balance, contact and useful whole-body behavior
chapters.question: How does a robot keep moving when balance, terrain and contact conditions change?
chapters.summary: Locomotion combines fast feedback with decisions about where and when to make contact. Quadrupeds, bipeds and humanoids share core mechanics but have different stability margins, actuator limits and task requirements. The research frontier spans model-based optimization, learned motor policies, perception and motion priors. A convincing result explains both the controller and the physical conditions under which it operates.

sections.heading: Why legs create an underactuated system
sections.text: A floating robot body has no motor that directly pushes it through the world. It changes momentum through forces at contacts, and those contacts can appear or disappear. Joint torques influence the body indirectly through the mechanism and ground. This creates coupled questions: which foot supports weight, what force can friction sustain, and which motion will make the next contact possible? A center-of-mass model can simplify planning, while a whole-body controller must still respect joint limits, torque limits and coordination across the mechanism.

sections.heading: MPC and learned policies solve different subproblems
sections.text: The MIT Cheetah 3 work uses a simplified body model to optimize contact forces online. That provides an interpretable objective and an explicit prediction horizon, with performance depending on the model and contact assumptions. Hwangbo and colleagues demonstrate policies learned in simulation and deployed on ANYmal. Learned policies can encode complex responses with cheap runtime evaluation, but expensive training and deployment mismatch remain. A fair comparison matches robot hardware, observations, command distributions and disturbances. Hybrid systems can use learning for adaptation while retaining optimization for selected constraints.

sections.heading: Perception must be useful under failure
sections.text: Proprioception reports the robot’s own motion; exteroception looks outward at terrain. Seeing a step early enables anticipation, but depth estimates may be absent, delayed or misleading. Miki and colleagues study how learned recurrence combines these information streams during outdoor locomotion. This is a control-relevant perception problem: an attractive terrain map is not enough if the policy trusts it when it is wrong. Evaluate dropout, calibration error and deformable surfaces separately from ordinary rough terrain. State which terrain information is available at training and at deployment.

sections.heading: Humanoids connect movement to manipulation
sections.text: A humanoid must do more than replay a plausible gait. Hands can carry loads, interact with the environment and alter balance; reaching may require stepping. Motion-capture priors offer examples of coordinated behavior, while retargeting translates between different bodies and actuator capabilities. AMP learns style rewards for simulated characters from motion clips. Its relevance to humanoid learning is conceptual and methodological; the original paper does not establish physical-robot transfer. Natural-looking motion, task accomplishment and mechanically feasible contact forces are three separate evaluation targets.

sections.heading: From an impressive demonstration to a research claim
sections.text: Characterize the operating envelope: speed, payload, terrain, battery condition, disturbance magnitude and observation failures. Recovery should include how the robot detects trouble and whether a human resets it. Energy use, foot slip and contact impact can reveal costs hidden by success rate. Suitable graduate projects isolate one interface, such as adapting to delay, using uncertain terrain estimates or combining hand contact with balance. Begin in simulation, then specify what a hardware test would need to validate; a simulation-only study can be valuable when its claim remains explicit.

open_questions: How can a controller adapt to morphology or actuator changes without unsafe exploration?
What information should a policy retain when external perception becomes unreliable?
How should locomotion and hand-contact objectives share a limited actuation budget?
pitfalls: Using simulated human-like animation as proof of robot hardware capability.
Comparing controllers on different robots without accounting for hardware.
Reporting only successful selected traversals instead of a defined test set.

project.title: Terrain perception under controlled corruption
project.description: On a simulated legged benchmark, compare a proprioceptive policy with a terrain-aware policy while injecting missing or biased terrain observations. Keep actuator and command settings fixed.
evaluation: Fall rate and tracking error across corruption levels.
Energy and foot-slip measures where available.
Training seeds, recovery behavior and worst observed conditions.

chapters.title: Simulation, world models and transfer
chapters.subtitle: Learning with an imperfect substitute for the world
chapters.question: Which inaccuracies can a controller tolerate, and which ones invalidate a simulated result?
chapters.summary: Simulation allows repeatable experiments and cheaper exploration, but a controller can exploit the simulator’s mistakes as easily as its useful structure. Transfer is therefore a problem about mismatches and evidence. Physics simulation, randomized training and learned world models offer different tools. Their value depends on what is modeled, what the policy must predict, and how the final claim is tested outside the training setting.

sections.heading: Name the mismatch before choosing the remedy
sections.text: Separate appearance, geometry, dynamics, sensing and task-distribution differences. A realistic image does not imply accurate friction; accurate rigid-body dynamics does not imply correct actuator delay. Contact compliance, backlash, calibration and control frequency may dominate a particular task. Write down which variations affect success and which are nuisance factors. This turns the vague reality gap into testable hypotheses. A good simulation study explains why its abstractions preserve the decision being investigated and which physical conclusions remain outside its evidence.

sections.heading: Randomization, identification and adaptation
sections.text: Visual domain randomization varies rendering conditions to make perception less dependent on one appearance, as in Tobin and colleagues’ localization study. Dynamics randomization varies physical parameters, as in Peng and colleagues’ arm-pushing work. System identification instead estimates parameters from measurements; online adaptation attempts to use recent experience as conditions change. These approaches can be combined. Broad randomization can sacrifice nominal performance or omit the actual failure mechanism. An observation history may help infer hidden dynamics, but robustness across models and identification of the correct model are different capabilities.

sections.heading: A learned world model is judged by its decisions
sections.text: A world model predicts consequences in a learned representation, potentially including rewards and termination. Dreamer trains behavior using imagined trajectories in this representation. This can reduce the need to gather a physical sample for every policy update, but prediction errors can compound or favor actions whose consequences are poorly known. Photorealistic video alone does not establish an action-conditioned dynamics model. Evaluate whether predictions distinguish the actions that matter, whether uncertainty is useful, and whether a policy trained against the model remains effective in the actual environment.

sections.heading: Cross-robot transfer is another mismatch
sections.text: Sharing data across embodiments introduces different sensors, action spaces and mechanical capabilities. Open X-Embodiment studies standardized data and joint training; Octo explicitly supports adapting observation and action interfaces. A common token representation does not make a torque command equivalent to an end-effector displacement. Useful transfer may come from visual semantics, task structure or low-level behavior, and each requires a different test. Hold out the robot or interface you claim to generalize to, disclose target adaptation data, and compare with an equally resourced model trained on that target data alone.

sections.heading: Design a transfer ladder
sections.text: Begin with repeatability in one simulator, then test untrained parameter settings and, where useful, a different simulator. This can reveal brittle assumptions but still does not establish hardware transfer. A real-system stage should record calibration, limits, interventions and data used to tune the simulator. Keep a final test condition untouched by tuning. For a student project, a carefully analyzed negative transfer result can be more informative than a polished success video: identify the missing mechanism, reproduce the failure, and show which modeling or control change actually repairs it.

open_questions: Which simulator parameters matter enough to identify rather than randomize?
How can model uncertainty prevent policies from exploiting inaccurate predictions?
When does shared robot data cause negative transfer, and how can it be detected?
pitfalls: Calling sim-to-sim evaluation sim-to-real transfer.
Using real test failures repeatedly to tune training while still calling the test held out.
Equating visually convincing generated video with physically correct actionable predictions.

project.title: A transfer failure map
project.description: Train a simple simulated pushing policy under three regimes: nominal dynamics, dynamics randomization, and a model fitted from a small calibration dataset. Evaluate on untouched parameter combinations.
evaluation: Success heatmaps over friction, mass and delay.
Nominal performance versus worst-case performance.
Calibration-data cost and failures outside the randomized ranges.

chapters.title: Benchmarks, reproducibility and research evidence
chapters.subtitle: Turning a demonstration into a defensible claim
chapters.question: What evidence would convince you that a result is useful, reproducible and relevant to your proposed research?
chapters.summary: A benchmark score is an answer to a particular experimental question, not a universal measure of robot intelligence. Good evaluation makes that question explicit: which tasks, robots, observations, training data and disturbances are included? For graduate applications, learning to interrogate evidence is more useful than sorting professors by citations. It helps you identify a lab’s scientific habits and formulate a credible problem of your own.

sections.heading: Match the claim to the test
sections.text: In-distribution success, a new object, an unfamiliar room, a new task composition and a new robot are different kinds of generalization. RLBench supplies a reusable simulated manipulation environment; LIBERO organizes transfer and continued-learning questions; FurnitureBench emphasizes reproducible long-horizon physical assembly. Choose the benchmark because its variation tests your claim. A method that excels on familiar object instances may still fail on changed geometry. Report what the split excludes and what information each model receives, including privileged state or task identifiers.

sections.heading: Count the entire experiment
sections.text: Record demonstrations, unsuccessful data, human corrections, resets, simulator interactions, training compute and hyperparameter searches. Compare the whole resource budget, not only the final network size. Dataset versions also matter: DROID’s official releases have changed annotations and calibration, and primary descriptions report different collection totals. BridgeData V2 documents another collection regime with different platform and environment coverage. Pin the exact release and transformations used. A familiar dataset name is not sufficient to establish that two papers evaluated the same problem.

sections.heading: Uncertainty belongs beside the score
sections.text: Twenty successful trials out of twenty do not prove perfect reliability. Report trial counts and uncertainty, and distinguish repeated test episodes from independent training runs. Reusing one trained model across many episodes does not measure variability caused by training randomness. Agarwal and colleagues show how point estimates can change algorithm rankings in deep RL and advocate interval estimates, performance profiles and robust aggregation. For robotics, also group outcomes by meaningful task or environment units; many nearly identical resets should not masquerade as broad independent coverage.

sections.heading: Ablations should challenge the explanation
sections.text: If a paper attributes improvement to a new policy architecture, ask whether data, perception, compute and tuning were matched. Remove the proposed component, retain a strong simple baseline, and inspect failure categories rather than only the average. Robomimic demonstrates why demonstration quality and checkpoint selection deserve explicit attention. Code and data releases make checking easier, but availability is not proof that a result reproduces. Distinguish an author-reported result, a runnable artifact, your reproduction and independent replication by another group.

sections.heading: Reading quality without outsourcing judgment
sections.text: Peer review, a respected venue and influential citations are useful context. None certifies that a particular claim is correct or that a lab fits your interests. Identify the contribution type: theory, algorithm, system, dataset or measurement. A system paper may be strong because it exposes a reproducible integration problem; a theory paper may be strong under assumptions far from your deployment. Read the limitations, inspect baselines and follow the released artifacts. In this encyclopedia, evidence depth describes what was checked for the summary; it never means the listed experiments were independently reproduced.

open_questions: Which test suite predicts useful performance outside a benchmark’s collection process?
How should long-horizon partial success and recovery be measured without obscuring failure?
What minimum reporting standard enables a small lab to reproduce a large-model result?
pitfalls: Treating a venue or citation total as a paper-quality verdict.
Pooling correlated trials while reporting an overly confident success rate.
Comparing benchmark scores across different splits, versions or observation modes.

project.title: Audit and reproduce one narrow claim
project.description: Choose one released manipulation baseline, reproduce a small fixed evaluation, then change one documented condition such as camera appearance or initial-state range. Publish a concise experiment card.
evaluation: Exact code, data and configuration versions.
Per-task results, run counts and uncertainty estimates.
A matched baseline, failure examples and an explicit boundary on the conclusion.

glossary.definition: An experiment that changes or removes a component to test its contribution while controlling other factors. It is strongest when designed to challenge a specific causal explanation.
Predicting a sequence of future actions together. The prediction horizon and the number of actions actually executed before receiving fresh feedback need not be the same.
Choosing an action partly to obtain better information, such as changing viewpoint before grasping. It couples sensing objectives with motion and task costs.
An action opportunity relative to an agent and situation, such as whether a handle can be grasped. A semantic object label alone does not establish a usable affordance.
A convergence property under stated assumptions: as computation or sample count grows without bound, solution cost approaches an optimum. It is not a fixed-deadline guarantee.

States from which a target set can be reached within a specified horizon under selected control/disturbance quantifiers. For failure targets, it helps characterize when avoidance is or is not possible.
Supervised fitting of a policy to demonstrated actions. Its simplicity makes it a valuable baseline; errors can compound when the deployed policy changes the observations it encounters.
A probability distribution over possible physical states conditioned on available information. It can serve as the decision state when the physical state is only partially observed.
An architecture in which learning uses team-level information while each deployed agent acts from its permitted local inputs. Test-time access to a central service changes that information model.
Evaluating a system while its actions affect subsequent observations and decisions. It reveals compounding errors and recovery behavior that isolated prediction metrics can miss.
A graph describing which agents can exchange information, possibly with directed, delayed, weighted, or time-varying links. It need not match the physical collision or sensing graph.
A condition requiring nonnegative quantities with zero product, so at least one is zero. In rigid contact models it can encode the relationship between separation and contact force.
The set of configurations describing a robot's pose or shape. An obstacle in physical space excludes a region of configuration space that depends on the robot's geometry.

A process through which interacting agents approach agreement on a quantity. Convergence depends on assumptions such as connectivity and update rules; it does not by itself solve task allocation or collision avoidance.
A qualitative relationship such as separation, sticking, sliding or rolling between bodies. Mode changes can alter both the equations of motion and the available control strategies.
A state-dependent or constant measure of infinitesimal distance under which nearby trajectories converge. Establishing the metric's validity and domain is part of the analysis.
A function that encodes a safe set and provides input-dependent inequalities sufficient for its forward invariance under stated regularity, model and feasibility assumptions.
The ability, within a specified dynamics model and input class, to steer the state between states. Linear controllability is distinct from having one actuator per mechanical degree of freedom.
A difference between the observation distribution in demonstrations and the one produced by the learned policy. In sequential control, the policy’s own mistakes can create the shift.
Deciding which measurements refer to the same landmark, object, or event. Incorrect associations can be more harmful than small numerical measurement errors.

A policy that generates actions or action sequences through conditional denoising. It can represent several plausible behaviors, while sampling speed and feedback frequency remain practical design choices.
Varying simulated conditions during training to reduce dependence on one nominal environment. Visual appearance randomization and physical dynamics randomization target different mismatches.
The physical and sensor–actuator configuration through which an agent acts. Different bodies change feasible movements, observations and the meaning of action commands.
A property in which transforming an input produces a corresponding transformation of the output. It differs from invariance, where the output remains unchanged.
Agreement between an estimator's reported uncertainty and its actual error statistics under the evaluation conditions. Small average error does not imply that its confidence is justified.
Measurements of the external environment, such as images or terrain depth. For control, usefulness depends on uncertainty, timing and whether the measurement predicts actionable conditions.
A representation that factors a joint probability or optimization objective into local relationships among variables. It exposes the sparse structure used by many smoothing and mapping algorithms.
Choosing an action using information about the system's observed or estimated behavior, so later actions can respond to deviations from the objective.
A set of contact-force directions consistent with a simplified friction model. It constrains how much tangential force a contact can support relative to normal loading.

A transformation of the estimated variables that leaves the available measurements unchanged, such as a common global translation in some mapping problems. It reflects missing absolute information rather than numerical noise.

Linking representations such as words, plans, or symbols to observations and executable capabilities. Grounded reasoning must account for what the robot can actually identify, reach, change, and verify.

Guidance selects desired motion; navigation estimates the vehicle's state; control commands forces or torques to execute the motion. Real missions couple these through uncertainty, constraints and timing.
For a stable linear system, a measure of the largest energy amplification from designated input disturbances to designated outputs. The chosen channels and weights define the performance claim.
An evaluation in which real hardware interacts with a simulated part of the system. Its evidential value depends on which components and physical effects are real, simulated or omitted.
Testing on data or conditions kept separate from training and model selection. The unit held out—episode, object, scene, task or robot—defines which generalization claim the test can support.

Control that shapes how motion responds to interaction forces, often through desired spring-like and damping behavior. Useful compliance depends on the complete actuator, sensing and control implementation.
The difference between an incoming measurement and its predicted value. Its magnitude and statistical structure can help diagnose incorrect models, sensor faults or inconsistent uncertainty.
Planning that accounts for both geometric constraints and differential constraints on motion, such as bounded acceleration or nonholonomic steering.
A space that combines smooth geometry with a compatible group operation. SO(3) represents rotations and SE(3) rigid poses, enabling geometry-aware estimation and control.
A local first-order approximation of nonlinear dynamics or measurements around an operating point or trajectory. Its validity is limited by how far the system moves from that reference.
Recognizing that a robot has returned to a previously observed place and adding a consistency constraint to its estimate. Incorrect recognition can introduce a damaging false constraint.
A reformulation or relaxation whose solution recovers a solution of an original nonconvex problem under specified conditions. It differs from solving a sequence of merely local convex approximations.
A positive energy-like scalar used to reason about stability through how it changes along trajectories. The required inequalities and the domain where they hold determine the resulting guarantee.
An RL formulation that rewards policy entropy along with task return. It promotes stochastic behavior during learning but does not ensure all useful states will be explored.
A reduction in target performance caused by sharing data, representations or training with another task or embodiment. It should be checked per target rather than hidden by an aggregate improvement.
The ability to distinguish states from their output histories under a model and known inputs. Unobservable directions cannot be recovered merely by increasing estimator computation.
Learning from transitions that can have been generated by behavior different from the policy being improved. Replay enables data reuse but creates estimation and distribution-mismatch challenges.
Learning primarily from data generated by the current or a recent policy, as in common PPO implementations. Updating the policy changes which data will be collected next.
Perception queried or organized using a broad set of language concepts rather than only a fixed training-label list. The term does not imply unlimited recognition or calibrated uncertainty.

A condition requiring sufficiently informative input or regressor variation over time to identify unknown parameters. A system can track well while lacking the excitation needed for parameter convergence.
A rule or model that maps available observations, history or state estimates to actions. Its interface matters: an action may be a torque, joint target, end-effector command or higher-level choice.

Information available during training or expert generation but unavailable to the deployed controller, such as ground-truth state or complete maps. Its use must be distinguished from deployment inputs.
Measurements related to the robot’s own state, such as joint positions, velocities and inertial signals. These measurements support feedback even when outward-looking perception becomes unreliable.
Repeatedly planning over a limited future horizon, executing part of the plan, and replanning from updated information. Its behavior depends on the model, horizon, constraints, and fallback.

The property that a feasible control problem remains feasible at later steps when the prescribed policy is applied and the stated assumptions hold. It is central to constrained receding-horizon control.
The set of initial states from which a specified closed-loop system converges to a target equilibrium or invariant behavior. A verified inner approximation may be smaller than the true region.

The accumulated reward over an episode or future horizon, often discounted. High return means the specified reward was optimized; it does not by itself establish that all physical requirements were satisfied.
A structured representation of entities and relations, potentially including geometry, containment, support, and semantic descriptions. Different edges can have different evidential status.
The elapsed time from a physical event or sensor acquisition to the resulting control action. It includes acquisition, processing, communication, scheduling, and actuator response.
Deploying a method developed or trained in simulation on a physical system. Differences in sensing, dynamics, contacts, timing, and environment can limit transfer.

A set of variables sufficient to predict a modeled system's future from its present state and future inputs. Sufficiency depends on the model; position alone usually omits velocity, bias or internal dynamics.
Estimating a system’s model or parameters from observations and inputs. It complements robust control and randomization when some uncertainty can be reduced with informative measurements.
Joint reasoning about discrete task choices and continuous geometric motions, including dependencies between object manipulation, grasp selection, placement, and reachability.

A formal language for properties involving time, such as always avoiding danger or eventually responding to an event. A specification is meaningful together with its model and environmental assumptions.
A time-indexed sequence of states or configurations. Unlike an untimed path, it exposes velocities, accelerations, and timing constraints that affect execution.
Having fewer independent actuation directions than configuration degrees of freedom at a given modeling level. A floating legged body is moved indirectly through joint motion and contact forces.

A policy value function gives expected future return, or cost-to-go, when following a specified policy. The optimal value function optimizes that quantity over admissible policies. State-value and action-value functions differ in whether the initial action is specified. Learned critics approximate these quantities; they are not safety certificates.
A model that connects visual and language inputs to robot action outputs. Its capabilities depend on action data, embodiment, action representation, and the surrounding execution system.

A predictive model of consequences, often in a learned latent representation. For control, its key test is whether action-conditioned predictions support better decisions, not only plausible reconstructions.

concept_edges.label: From equilibrium to gait
concept_edges.explanation: Legged motion uses the same dynamics and feedback principles, but periodic motion and contact require reasoning about orbits, impacts and changing support rather than only a fixed equilibrium.

concept_edges.label: From state to trajectory and map
concept_edges.explanation: Filtering supplies the inference language; smoothing and factor graphs extend it to jointly estimate motion and environmental structure from repeated observations.

concept_edges.label: Measurements need a likelihood
concept_edges.explanation: When a vision network feeds a model-based navigation stack, its geometry, uncertainty, timing and failure modes must be reflected in the estimator's measurement model. Direct visuomotor policies can use visual inputs without a separate explicit estimator, but their sensing assumptions and failure modes still need closed-loop evaluation.

concept_edges.label: Add dynamics to a route
concept_edges.explanation: A collision-free path becomes executable only when time, actuation and dynamical constraints are considered. Trajectory optimization connects geometric route choice to feasible motion.

concept_edges.label: A shared language of value
concept_edges.explanation: Value functions and policies connect optimal control to reinforcement learning. The difference often lies in how dynamics and costs are known or learned, not in whether actions affect a physical system.

concept_edges.label: Optimization can generate demonstrations
concept_edges.explanation: An optimizer can supply expert trajectories or warm-start targets. Imitation must still address what happens when a learned policy visits states absent from those demonstrations.

concept_edges.label: Contact is a decision variable
concept_edges.explanation: Manipulation combines continuous motion with contact creation, sticking and separation. Complementarity and hybrid trajectory formulations expose those choices instead of assuming a fixed contact sequence.

concept_edges.label: The transfer gap is model uncertainty
concept_edges.explanation: Robustness and adaptation provide ways to describe discrepancies between simulation and hardware. Randomization should target consequential deployment variation; coverage alone is not a robustness guarantee, and any claimed extrapolation beyond the training distribution requires separate evaluation.

concept_edges.label: Local guarantees must compose
concept_edges.explanation: A safe action for one agent can depend on another agent's behavior. Multi-agent safety requires compatible assumptions, interaction models and enough control authority to resolve conflicts.

concept_edges.label: Audit the interfaces of a learned stack
concept_edges.explanation: An embodied policy depends on perception, memory and action execution. Safety reasoning asks which module assumptions are checked and whether a fallback remains available when those assumptions fail.

concept_edges.label: A theorem and a test answer different questions
concept_edges.explanation: Proofs cover modeled assumptions; experiments test implementations and expose omissions. A useful evaluation records both the certified domain and empirical failures beyond it.

concept_edges.label: Mission autonomy under limited recovery
concept_edges.explanation: Spacecraft and field robots share uncertain sensing, constrained energy and incomplete maps. Their physical models differ, so transfer the decomposition and validation discipline while rebuilding domain assumptions.

concept_edges.label: A plan becomes a constrained optimization problem
concept_edges.explanation: Trajectory planning assigns costs and feasibility constraints to motions. Optimal-control tools add dynamics and timing, while search helps expose alternative routes and task choices that local optimization may miss.

concept_edges.label: Contact and object choices reshape the search space
concept_edges.explanation: Manipulation planning must choose grasps, placements, and contact modes as well as motions. Moving an object changes future reachability, making task and motion planning a natural bridge.

concept_edges.label: A map is a coupled state estimate
concept_edges.explanation: SLAM jointly infers motion and environmental structure. Observability, calibration, data association, and uncertainty propagation explain both its successes and its failure modes.

concept_edges.label: The policy learns through its observation representation
concept_edges.explanation: Imitation from images depends on what the perception system preserves about geometry, objects, and contact. A perceptual shortcut can fit demonstrations while failing when the scene or viewpoint changes.

concept_edges.label: Operating conditions test model uncertainty
concept_edges.explanation: Wind, slip, timing variation, and sensing degradation expose uncertainty beyond nominal dynamics. Robust-control reasoning helps identify which disturbances a deployed feedback loop can tolerate.

concept_edges.label: Remote autonomy shares delayed feedback and limited recovery
concept_edges.explanation: Field and space robots both face uncertain environments, resource constraints, and restricted intervention. The transferable ideas are estimation, planning, and fault management; flight dynamics and mission assumptions still require separate treatment.

concept_edges.label: Traversability connects sensing to physical capability
concept_edges.explanation: A terrain map becomes useful only when interpreted relative to a robot's locomotion limits. Slopes, footholds, friction, and stability determine whether a visually open route is physically traversable.

concept_edges.label: Training assumptions must survive deployment
concept_edges.explanation: Simulation can supply privileged states and many trials, but physical sensing, dynamics, and timing differ. Transfer studies should isolate these gaps and include recovery rather than only nominal success.

concept_edges.label: Networks extend feedback beyond one robot
concept_edges.explanation: Consensus and formation control connect linear systems, graph structure, and feedback. Explicit assumptions about connectivity, delay, and local measurements determine what team-level conclusions follow.

concept_edges.label: Local safety constraints interact with team progress
concept_edges.explanation: Collision-avoidance constraints can modify each agent's proposed action, but a collision-free team may still deadlock. Safety and progress require separate arguments and joint experimental assessment.

concept_edges.label: Skill values can ground semantic choices
concept_edges.explanation: Value estimates can help rank which skills are likely to succeed in a state, providing one bridge from language-level relevance to physical capability. Their calibration and training distribution remain central limitations.

concept_edges.label: Task reasoning needs episode-level evidence
concept_edges.explanation: A plausible plan or fluent explanation does not establish execution. Full-episode evaluation must expose resets, retries, missing skills, intervention, and the type of generalization being claimed.

concept_edges.label: Objectives connect control and learning
concept_edges.explanation: Optimal control and RL both choose behavior against an objective. They differ in available models, data and computation, and can share a controller rather than form mutually exclusive camps.

concept_edges.label: Uncertainty defines the transfer problem
concept_edges.explanation: Robustness and adaptation provide ways to describe discrepancies between simulation and hardware. Randomization should target consequential deployment variation; coverage alone is not a robustness guarantee, and any claimed extrapolation beyond the training distribution requires separate evaluation.

concept_edges.label: History can serve control-relevant inference
concept_edges.explanation: A recurrent policy can use observation history to respond to hidden state or changing dynamics. Explicit estimation adds interpretable hypotheses and uncertainty; the two approaches should be compared on the same information.

concept_edges.label: Reward is different from a constraint
concept_edges.explanation: Reward penalties guide preferences, whereas safety constraints restrict acceptable behavior. Their combination raises questions about feasibility, model uncertainty and interventions.

concept_edges.label: Interaction reveals what images hide
concept_edges.explanation: Contact can disambiguate geometry, friction or object state. Tactile and force feedback therefore connect perception directly to the choice of manipulation actions.

concept_edges.label: Long tasks need skill sequencing and recovery
concept_edges.explanation: Task and motion planning connects symbolic progress with geometric feasibility. Learned contact skills still need conditions for invocation, completion and recovery.

concept_edges.label: Terrain tests the entire autonomy stack
concept_edges.explanation: Field locomotion depends on perception, state estimation and motor control together. A terrain traversal result should reveal which part handles degraded sensing or unexpected contacts.

concept_edges.label: Semantics needs an action interface
concept_edges.explanation: Language-conditioned models can select meaningful goals, but useful embodied behavior also needs actions with the correct units, timing and physical affordances.

concept_edges.label: Limited physical access increases model scrutiny
concept_edges.explanation: Space systems make realistic repeated interaction difficult. Simulation and learned models can be useful, but transfer claims require attention to operating conditions and validation standards specific to the mission.

concept_edges.label: Shared experience creates correlated evidence
concept_edges.explanation: Multi-agent and fleet data may enlarge a dataset while retaining shared environmental biases. Evaluation should distinguish genuinely different operating conditions from repeated correlated observations.

concept_edges.label: Mapping is valuable only with timely uncertainty
concept_edges.explanation: Localization and terrain maps support locomotion, but drift and stale estimates can mislead contact decisions. Control evaluation should include how map uncertainty reaches the policy.

concept_edges.label: Probability turns successes into evidence
concept_edges.explanation: A finite test set estimates performance with uncertainty. Experimental units, dependence and the target distribution determine what the reported success rate can justify.

paths.title: From control to autonomy
paths.description: For a dynamics or aerospace background: connect models and feedback to perception, planning and uncertainty.
outcomes: Explain the state, inputs and constraints of a physical system.
Build and diagnose a state estimator.
Compare tracking with constrained receding-horizon control.
Turn goals into feasible motions.
Integrate perception with decisions on a mobile platform.
State exactly which disturbances and failures your safety claim covers.

paths.title: Into robot learning
paths.description: Understand how policies learn, where data come from, and why physical evaluation changes the problem.
outcomes: Separate a robot’s state from what sensors observe.
Explain rewards, exploration and policy improvement.
Compare demonstrated behavior with reward-based learning.
Identify the assumptions behind transfer.
Evaluate contact, dexterity and recovery.
Design a comparison that can survive a change of robot or environment.

paths.title: Spacecraft guidance & control
paths.description: Follow navigation and optimization into mission-scale decisions without losing the physical model.
outcomes: Write a tractable vehicle model and identify what it leaves out.
Connect measurement errors to navigation uncertainty.
Distinguish adaptation from a robust bound.
Check dynamics, constraints and solver timing together.
Evaluate a rendezvous or landing case under dispersions.
Explain why a simulation success rate is not a flight safety guarantee.

paths.title: Humanoids & dexterity
paths.description: Connect hybrid dynamics, optimization, learned control and contact-rich behavior.
outcomes: Identify contact modes and actuation limits.
Understand how optimization coordinates many joints.
Separate locomotion stability from task success.
Recognize the role of simulation and reward design.
Compare whole-body and dexterous contact strategies.
Report interventions, failures and transfer limits.

paths.title: Spatial & embodied intelligence
paths.description: Start with representations of the world, then connect them to grounded actions.
outcomes: Ask which information a representation preserves.
Track uncertainty instead of a single confident guess.
Understand consistency and loop closure.
Connect geometry to feasible actions.
Separate language understanding from physical execution.
Assess whether a policy can recover outside demonstrations.

paths.title: Learn to judge a research claim
paths.description: A method for reading papers and choosing research questions across disciplinary boundaries.
outcomes: Locate the exact claim and its evidence.
Inspect the assumptions behind a guarantee.
Distinguish average performance from worst-case behavior.
Test transfer under the shifts that matter.
Separate coordination benefits from communication assumptions.
Evaluate whether system-level success is grounded or merely plausible.

loop.title: Observe
loop.text: Sensors measure images, forces, motion and signals.

loop.title: Estimate
loop.text: Infer the hidden state and quantify uncertainty.

loop.title: Decide
loop.text: Choose goals, actions and feasible trajectories.

loop.title: Act
loop.text: Use feedback to influence a changing physical world.

loop.title: Learn
loop.text: Improve models, representations or policies from experience.
